Huot family · one man's places · 1827 to 1893

Louis Huot's Movements

Where Louis Huot was, year by year, from his baptism on the Beaupré coast below Quebec to his death on the Red Lake River in Minnesota, and how each place is known. A solid bar means a record puts him there. A pale bar means the place rests on his obituary or a later account. A hatched bar means nothing says where he was.

    Five periods

    The whole route

    From the Beaupré coast below Quebec, by way of Detroit in 1849 to the Falls of St. Anthony, out to a farm at Medicine Lake, on to Corcoran, and in 1876 north to the Red Lake River.

    Choose a period above to follow one stretch of his life: the map moves to where he lived and draws the line up to that time.

    Period by period

    No.PeriodWhere he livedWhat the records showHow firmStill open
    1 L'Ange-Gardien1827 to 1849A farmer's son L'Ange-Gardien, on the Beaupré coast below Quebec. Baptized in the next parish, Château-Richer. Born 1 May 1827, baptized the next day, son of François Huot, farmer of L'Ange-Gardien, and Angélique Breton. His father was buried there on 19 Aug 1833, when Louis was six. His mother married Prisque Noël there on 12 Apr 1836. Firm for 1827. Nothing names Louis between his baptism and his landing at Detroit; his parents' acts keep the household in the parish. When he left, and with whom. No record shows a brother or sister travelling with him in 1849.
    2 St. Anthony1849 to about 1858Stone mason The Falls of St. Anthony, now north-east Minneapolis, at first in Pierre Bottineau's household. Landed at Detroit on 3 Aug 1849. Declared his intention at St. Paul on 31 Aug 1850 and was counted at St. Anthony two weeks later, a stone mason of 25. Married Marguerite Raiche on 31 Aug 1852; Onesime was born in 1853 and Philomene in 1854. Marguerite died on 26 Nov 1854. He married Henriette Patnode on 8 Apr 1856, and Louise was born in 1857. Firm to September 1850. After that the marriages and baptisms are in the St. Anthony parish register, which does not say where the family lived. His obituary says he was a mason for ten years. Sixteen months, from Marguerite's death to the second marriage, have no record at all. One family account says he went back to Canada in that time. Marguerite's burial has not been found, and the stone on her grave carries another surname and the year 1851.
    3 Medicine Lakeabout 1858 to about 1862Farmer Section 15 of Plymouth township, Hennepin County, by Medicine Lake. Patent dated 10 Mar 1860 for 160 acres in section 15, taken up with a bounty land warrant he had bought from a War of 1812 widow. Counted at Plymouth on 15 Oct 1860, a farmer with real estate of $800, with Henriette and four children. Four other Huot households stood within six dwellings. Firm for 1860. That he was there from 1858 or 1859 rests on his obituary and on later accounts of the log church, built on land bought from him. When he moved out from St. Anthony. The obituary says 1859; a family account says 1854. The land entry papers for the warrant would give the date.
    4 Corcoranby 1863 to 1876Retail liquor dealer, merchant, farmer Corcoran township, Hennepin County, north-west of Medicine Lake. Licensed to sell liquor at Corcoran from 1 May 1863, and called a merchant on the draft list that summer. Tax entries follow in 1864, 1865 and 1866. Counted at Corcoran in 1870 and 1875 with ten children at home. Treasurer of the French Canadian society at Medina in 1871. Asked for as administrator of Michel Patnode's estate in 1868. Henriette died on 28 Jul 1875. Firm from May 1863 to May 1875. A Quebec notary's act of 14 Mar 1865 has a Louis Huot, merchant, acting for the heirs of his late wife Margaret and naming an attorney in Hennepin County. That he is this Louis is probable and not proved. When he left Plymouth for Corcoran, between October 1860 and May 1863. Whether he was in Quebec in the spring of 1865. Henriette's death has no record.
    5 Huot1876 to 1893Ferryman, postmaster, town clerk, homesteader The Old Crossing of the Red Lake River, section 28 of Louisville township, then Polk County. The place took his name. Signed the application for a post office on 30 Dec 1880, with "Louisville" struck out and "Huot" written in. Appointed postmaster on 3 Aug 1881. Naturalized at Crookston on 18 Jun 1883 and patented his homestead in August 1884. In December 1892 he and his brother Edouard went to Chicago, called to a brother who was gravely ill. He died on 4 Mar 1893. Firm from December 1880. The move north in 1876, six weeks by ox wagon, rests on his obituary and a family account. The year of the move, 1875 or 1876. Which brother was ill at Chicago.

    The records themselves

    The pages the dates come from, in order. The Quebec acts are given in words only. French and Latin acts are given as written and then in English; the spelling is the clerk's. Choose an image to see it full size.

    What is open

    1. When did he move to Medicine Lake? His obituary, printed twelve days after he died, says he farmed there from 1859 after ten years as a mason. A family account puts the move just before Marguerite's death in November 1854. The warrant he used was issued under an act of 3 March 1855, so that land cannot have been entered before then. The land entry papers for warrant 41,304 at the National Archives carry the date it was located.
    2. Was he in Quebec between November 1854 and April 1856? One family account says so. His brother Edouard gave 1855 as his own year of arrival and stood witness at Louis's wedding in April 1856, which would fit Louis having gone home and come back with him. That reading rests on two dates and nothing else.
    3. Is the Louis Huot of the 1865 act this Louis? For it: a late wife Margaret whose children he acts for, an attorney named William Dugas at Bottineau Prairie when a William Dugas was godfather to Louis's daughter in 1854, land scrip under a Chippewa treaty, and the word "merchant". Against it: the act calls him "of the parish of L'Ange Gardien". His liquor licence that December runs from the first of the month, which fits a business that had lapsed, and shows nothing more. The land office record of the scrip would name the holder and his attorney together.
    4. What the scrip says about Marguerite. Scrip under the La Pointe treaty of 30 Sept 1854 went to people of mixed Chippewa descent. If the act is his, Louis held eighty acres of it for Marguerite's children. That points toward her family's origins and proves nothing yet.
    5. Whose name is on Marguerite's stone? The grave at Medicine Lake is marked "Begin Marguerite, wife of L. Huot, Nov 26 1851, age of 22 years", on a modern granite stone. The registers have Louis's wife as Marguerite Raiche, married in 1852 and a mother in 1853 and 1854. The likeliest reading is that an older marker or list was miscopied when the stone was replaced, the surname and the last figure of the year both. It has not been shown. A grave at Medicine Lake would also bear on when the family moved there. The parish's lot record for row 10, lot 4, and a burial entry for November 1854, would settle it.
    6. The moves to Corcoran and to the north are each dated only by his obituary and by family accounts.

    The places on the map

    What the records tell us about each place, in the order he came to them.

    • L'Ange-Gardien

      Beaupré coast, Montmorency County, Quebec

      His parents' parish. They married here on 10 Feb 1823. His father, François Huot, was buried here on 19 Aug 1833 and his mother, Angélique Breton, on 18 May 1866. Neither parent came to Minnesota.

    • Château-Richer

      The next parish down the coast

      Louis was baptized here on 2 May 1827, "né la veille". One priest served both parishes in those years and entered an act in whichever register he had with him.

    • Quebec City

      Office of the notary François Huot, 14 Mar 1865

      A Louis Huot, merchant, "of the parish of L'Ange Gardien", gave William Dugas of Bottineau Prairie, Hennepin County, power to locate and sell eighty acres of land scrip, acting for himself and for the children of his late wife Margaret. He signed his name. Probably this Louis; not proved.

    • Detroit

      Michigan, 3 Aug 1849

      Where he entered the United States, by his own sworn statement a year later. How he came from Quebec, and how he went on to Minnesota, is not recorded.

    • St. Paul

      Ramsey County court, 31 Aug 1850

      He declared his intention to become a citizen here, thirteen months after landing. He did not complete it until 1883.

    • St. Anthony

      The Falls, now north-east Minneapolis

      Counted here on 15 Sept 1850 in Pierre Bottineau's household, a stone mason. Both his marriages and the baptisms of Onesime, Philomene and Louise are in the register of St. Anthony of Padua. A newspaper of 1856 names a Huot among the French who settled the town in 1849.

    • Medicine Lake

      Section 15, Plymouth township, Hennepin County

      His 160 acres, patented on 10 Mar 1860. The log church of the French settlers stood on land bought from him, by later accounts in 1859 for $100. In October 1860 Francis, Edward, Elie and Oliver Huot all lived within six dwellings of him. The parish cemetery here holds the grave marked "Begin Marguerite, wife of L. Huot".

    • Corcoran

      Hennepin County, by May 1863

      Home for thirteen years. He kept a licensed liquor business, farmed, and raised ten children here with Henriette Patnode, whose own family were Corcoran settlers. She died here in 1875.

    • Huot

      Old Crossing of the Red Lake River, Louisville township

      He kept the ferry, the post office and the town's books. The office was to be called Louisville; the application has that struck out and "Huot" written in. He is buried here.

    • Crookston

      Polk County seat, 18 Jun 1883

      He was naturalized here, thirty-three years after his declaration at St. Paul. The mail for his post office came out from Crookston.

    • Chicago

      December 1892

      Louis and his brother Edouard were called here to a brother "dangerously ill" and were back in Minneapolis on 26 December. The paper does not name him. Louis died ten weeks later.

    • La Pointe

      Madeline Island, Wisconsin. Louis is not known to have been here.

      Where the United States made its treaty with the Chippewa of Lake Superior and the Mississippi on 30 Sept 1854. The land scrip in the 1865 act was issued under it.

    Sources: the parish registers of L'Ange-Gardien and Château-Richer (Drouin collection); the registers of St. Anthony of Padua, Minneapolis (Minnesota Genealogical Society films); United States and Minnesota censuses; naturalization records of Ramsey and Polk counties (Iron Range Research Center); General Land Office patents; Internal Revenue assessment lists; Post Office Department records; the greffe of the notary François Huot, Quebec; L'Echo de l'Ouest and the Minneapolis Tribune.
